catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemic. In a word base stress is always on the penultimate syllable. 'SS ['hi.ku] 'elbow' S'SS [mo.'u.ro] 'to groan' SS'SS [ma.ŋko.'lo.hi] 'virtues' SSS'SS [mo.ɭo.ɭi.'ta.i] 'to discuss' SSSS'SS [me.po.no.ho.'ri.i] 'to invite' SSSSS'SS [ma.mpo.ra.mba.i.'ki.i] 'to co-work in rice fields' Word bases include both content words (nouns, verbs, adverbs) and grammatical function words (prefixes and suffixes and multisyllabic enclitics). If a noun gets a possessive pronoun, the stress is moved to the penultimate syllable of the new word. ['ta.mbi] 'house' [ta.'mbi.ŋku] 'my house' ... Similary, when a verb gets an enclitic personal pronoun or an enclitic aspect marker, the stress is moved to the penultimate syllable of the new word base. [mo-.bo.'ku?.-mo] 'to-fracture-already' 'fractured' [pe.-o.ha?.'a.-ra] 'LOC-stay-3.pers.pl.' 'place where they stay'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (33 pp., HP scan + Acrobat scanned layer, 1,307,201 bytes) and rendered pdf pp. 19-20 to PNG. Pdf p. 19 carries the typescript page number 17 and p. 20 the number 18, so the locator is right. On the page image, under the heading '4.4 Suprasegmental items' / 'Stress', the text reads exactly: 'Stress is not phonemic. In a word base stress is always on the penultimate syllable.' followed by the six examples ['hi.ku] 'elbow', [mo.'u.ro] 'to groan', [ma.ŋko.'lo.hi] 'virtues', [mo.lo.li.'ta.i] 'to discuss', [me.po.no.ho.'ri.i] 'to invite', [ma.mpo.ra.mba.i.'ki.i] 'to co-work in rice fields'; then 'Word bases include both content words (nouns, verbs, adverbs) and grammatical function words…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive stress on the penultimate syllable of the word base; possessive pronouns, enclitic personal pronouns and enclitic aspect markers are counted in, so stress shifts rightward to remain penultimate in the enlarged word (examples with 2- to 7-syllable bases: ['hi.ku], [mo.'u.ro], [ma.ŋko.'lo.hi], [me.po.no.ho.'ri.i], [ma.mpo.ra.mba.i.'ki.i]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. The reviewer (René van den Berg, comments p. 4, item 15) asks 'do you have secondary stress? For instance on every second syllable to the left of the stressed syllable?' — left unanswered in this draft.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Long vowels are analysed as two-syllable sequences of like vowels because of the stress rule (section 5.1); the reviewer asks what happens when one of two like vowels is stressed, and whether all affixes/clitics shift stress or only some.
new_statements.domain_note: Word (word base plus possessive/enclitic pronouns and aspect enclitics); citation-form data from one speaker of the Rampi (Dodolo) village variety. Draft posted 'as is' without peer review; handwritten margin notes on the page ('word?' next to 'word base').
new_statements.identity_note: Christensen 1990 describes Rampi as spoken in Dodolo hamlet of desa Rampi (the authors lived in Onondowa; they note dialect differences between Rampi village and Leboni/Onondowa, and margin notes say some vowel contrasts do not hold in Onondowa). Grimes & Grimes 1987 treat Leboni as the prestige dialect. All fall under ramp1243 (no dialect glottocodes known).

sources.note: Survey-level only, Appendix E p. 93: 'Stress in South Sulawesi languages usually occurs on the penultimate syllable. In such cases it is not marked in the word lists.' The Rampi wordlist rows carry almost no stress marks (2 of 48 scanned rows contain an apostrophe), consistent with regular penultimate stress, but no Rampi-specific statement is made; the only Rampi phonetic note (p. 96) is the retroflexed lateral flap.
